title: Off Campus
synopsis: Junior year. A hockey scholarship. A part-time job. A roommate situation that is, depending on the day, a romance. You have eighteen credits and one heart. Choose what to spend them on.

nodes.text: The off-campus house is bigger and dustier than the brochure suggested. Your three teammates haul a couch. Your maybe-girlfriend Hannah arrives, surprising everyone but you, with a houseplant. Choose “Help her find a spot for the plant” and Bookstore comes into view; choose “Keep helping with the couch” and the road bends toward The Captain.

choices.text: Help her find a spot for the plant
choices.consequence: You help her find a spot for the plant. It carries you toward Bookstore and makes the feeling underneath the decision impossible to hide.
You choose to keep helping with the couch. The way to The Captain opens, trading the safety of ambiguity for the possibility of being understood.

nodes.text: Hannah and you wander the bookstore together. She buys a course pack. You buy a coffee. She holds your hand on the walk back like you've been together for a year. You haven't. “Talk about what 'this' is” draws you toward The Job; “Don't talk about it; let it be” leaves Hannah's Parents waiting on the other side.

choices.consequence: You commit to talk about what 'this' is. By The Job, the distance between you will have changed, even if neither of you names it.

choices.text: Don't talk about it; let it be
choices.consequence: You don't talk about it; let it be. It carries you toward Hannah's Parents and makes the feeling underneath the decision impossible to hide.

nodes.text: Coach picks the captain on Friday. You are runner-up. Garrett, who deserves it, gets it. You realize you are equal parts relieved and disappointed, which is the most honest you've felt about hockey in a year.

choices.consequence: You commit to be visibly happy for Garrett. By The Job, the distance between you will have changed, even if neither of you names it.
You choose to let yourself feel disappointed privately. The way to Hannah's Parents opens, trading the safety of ambiguity for the possibility of being understood.

nodes.text: Your part-time job at the campus bar starts. Tips are okay. The shift is until 2. Hockey practice is at 6 a.m. You realize you've signed up for, in the old phrase, the eighteen-hour day.

choices.consequence: You choose to drop a class to balance. The way to Midterms opens, trading the safety of ambiguity for the possibility of being understood.

choices.text: Push through; you can sleep in December
choices.consequence: You choose to push through; you can sleep in December. The way to The Tournament opens, trading the safety of ambiguity for the possibility of being understood.

nodes.text: Hannah's parents visit campus for a weekend. They invite you to dinner. You realize you are now, suddenly, in 'meet the parents' territory. They are nice. Her dad asks you about hockey statistics. The paths divide here: “Be honest about your stats” leads into Midterms, while “Be honest about your major” makes The Tournament the next reckoning.

choices.consequence: You be honest about your stats. It carries you toward Midterms and makes the feeling underneath the decision impossible to hide.
You choose to be honest about your major. The way to The Tournament opens, trading the safety of ambiguity for the possibility of being understood.

nodes.text: Three exams in a week. Your professor sees you fall asleep in lecture. He, kindly, does not call you out. He, kindly, also schedules you for office hours. To choose “Go to office hours” means meeting Garrett's Bad Stretch; “Skip; sleep instead” sends you toward Hannah's Friend instead.

choices.consequence: You go to office hours. It carries you toward Garrett's Bad Stretch and makes the feeling underneath the decision impossible to hide.
You choose to skip; sleep instead. The way to Hannah's Friend opens, trading the safety of ambiguity for the possibility of being understood.

nodes.text: A weekend tournament in Maine. You play well. Hannah cannot come. You text her between games. She is, you can tell, slightly bored of being texted between games. The paths divide here: “Call her after the late game” leads into Garrett's Bad Stretch, while “Sleep; she'll understand” makes Hannah's Friend the next reckoning.

choices.text: Call her after the late game
choices.consequence: You choose to call her after the late game. The way to Garrett's Bad Stretch opens, trading the safety of ambiguity for the possibility of being understood.
You choose to sleep; she'll understand. The way to Hannah's Friend opens, trading the safety of ambiguity for the possibility of being understood.

nodes.text: Garrett, the captain, is in a slump. Coach is on him. He, off-ice, doesn't talk to anyone. You realize captain isn't, mostly, a prize. It is a weight. The paths divide here: “Talk to Garrett one-on-one” leads into Coach's Office, while “Let him have his space” makes The Conversation the next reckoning.

choices.consequence: You talk to Garrett one-on-one. It carries you toward Coach's Office and makes the feeling underneath the decision impossible to hide.
You let him have his space. It carries you toward The Conversation and makes the feeling underneath the decision impossible to hide.

nodes.text: Hannah's friend Maya tells you, gently and without saying so directly, that Hannah is tired of being the one who initiates. You realize this is true. You realize you are also, possibly, the one who is tired.

choices.consequence: You commit to initiate something thoughtful this week. By Coach's Office, the distance between you will have changed, even if neither of you names it.

choices.text: Have a real conversation about it
choices.consequence: You commit to have a real conversation about it. By The Conversation, the distance between you will have changed, even if neither of you names it.

nodes.text: Coach calls you in. He wants to talk about whether you want hockey to be your life after graduation. He is honest about your ceiling. You realize you are honest with yourself for the first time about it too.

choices.text: Decide hockey is for college and beyond
choices.consequence: You choose to decide hockey is for college and beyond. The way to Finals opens, trading the safety of ambiguity for the possibility of being understood.

choices.text: Decide hockey is for college, period
choices.consequence: You choose to decide hockey is for college, period. The way to Career Fair opens, trading the safety of ambiguity for the possibility of being understood.

nodes.text: You sit on the porch with Hannah. The conversation is not perfect. The conversation is real. By the end you both know what the next month will be — and it is, surprisingly, more 'us' than you'd been managing.

choices.consequence: You choose to reset the relationship on purpose. The way to Finals opens, trading the safety of ambiguity for the possibility of being understood.
You take it week by week. It carries you toward Career Fair and makes the feeling underneath the decision impossible to hide.

nodes.text: Three finals. Two late shifts at the bar. One playoff game. You sleep, total, twelve hours. You survive the week and your roommate hands you a beer at midnight on Friday. It is, briefly, the best beer of your life.

choices.consequence: You go home for the break. It carries you toward Spring Semester and makes the feeling underneath the decision impossible to hide.
You stay in town with Hannah. It carries you toward Senior Captain Vote and makes the feeling underneath the decision impossible to hide.

nodes.text: You go to the career fair in a borrowed blazer. You hand out résumés. You realize the future is, against expectations, available. You also realize most of the recruiters at this fair are looking at hockey players for, of all things, sales.

choices.text: Talk to a tech company that interests you
choices.consequence: You choose to talk to a tech company that interests you. The way to Spring Semester opens, trading the safety of ambiguity for the possibility of being understood.

choices.text: Talk to the kind sales recruiter
choices.consequence: You talk to the kind sales recruiter. It carries you toward Senior Captain Vote and makes the feeling underneath the decision impossible to hide.

nodes.text: Spring is gentler. You drop a class. You take a writing class instead. The writing class is, embarrassingly, the best class you have taken in college. The distance between Senior Year and Graduation Day begins with the choice between “Pivot toward writing” and “Stay your major.”

choices.consequence: You pivot toward writing. It carries you toward Senior Year and makes the feeling underneath the decision impossible to hide.
You commit to stay your major. By Graduation Day, the distance between you will have changed, even if neither of you names it.

nodes.text: End of the year. Captains for next season are voted on. Your name is on the list. So is Garrett's, again. You realize you might, this time, want it. The distance between Senior Year and Graduation Day begins with the choice between “Accept the nomination” and “Decline and support Garrett.”

choices.consequence: You accept the nomination. It carries you toward Senior Year and makes the feeling underneath the decision impossible to hide.
You decline and support Garrett. It carries you toward Graduation Day and makes the feeling underneath the decision impossible to hide.

nodes.text: Senior year arrives. You are captain or you aren't. You and Hannah are still, somehow, together. Your professor invites you to TA the intro writing course. The houseplant is huge. Both choices lead to The Last Home Game, but “Take the TA job” arrives there with a different cost than “Focus only on hockey and Hannah.”

choices.consequence: You commit to take the TA job. By The Last Home Game, the distance between you will have changed, even if neither of you names it.

choices.text: Focus only on hockey and Hannah
choices.consequence: You focus only on hockey and Hannah. It carries you toward The Last Home Game and makes the feeling underneath the decision impossible to hide.

nodes.text: Cap and gown. Your family in the bleachers. Hannah ahead of you in line. Garrett behind you. Coach watching from the side. You realize, for one second, that this is the moment you'll think about when life is hard later.

choices.text: Take a mental photo to keep forever
choices.consequence: You take a mental photo to keep forever. It carries you toward The Apartment Lease and makes the feeling underneath the decision impossible to hide.

choices.text: Plan a road trip with Hannah for the summer
choices.consequence: You plan a road trip with Hannah for the summer. It carries you toward The Apartment Lease and makes the feeling underneath the decision impossible to hide.

nodes.text: Senior night. The rink lights, the parents standing, your name read over the PA. You realize this might be the last time you skate in front of people who came because of you. First Real Monday is already waiting. What changes is whether “Take it in fully” or “Play it like every other game” is the instinct you carry into it.

choices.consequence: You commit to take it in fully. By First Real Monday, the distance between you will have changed, even if neither of you names it.

choices.text: Play it like every other game
choices.consequence: You commit to play it like every other game. By First Real Monday, the distance between you will have changed, even if neither of you names it.

nodes.text: After graduation Hannah and you walk through a small apartment near the city. The kitchen tiles are ugly. The window has good light. You decide together what the year after college looks like. First Real Monday will follow either decision, but it will meet a different version of you after “Sign the lease” than after “Wait six months and travel first.”

choices.consequence: You commit to sign the lease. By First Real Monday, the distance between you will have changed, even if neither of you names it.

choices.text: Wait six months and travel first
choices.consequence: You commit to wait six months and travel first. By First Real Monday, the distance between you will have changed, even if neither of you names it.

nodes.text: First real Monday after college. The world is, finally, not a syllabus. You sit on a porch and look at it. You decide which version of your life starts now. Choose “Build the after” and After College comes into view; choose “Stay present for now” and the road bends toward The Long Saturday. A third choice, “Take the road trip first,” keeps Summer Road Trip in play.

choices.consequence: You choose to build the after. The way to After College opens, trading the safety of ambiguity for the possibility of being understood.
You commit to stay present for now. By The Long Saturday, the distance between you will have changed, even if neither of you names it.
You commit to take the road trip first. By Summer Road Trip, the distance between you will have changed, even if neither of you names it.

nodes.text: You finish college with options. You take a job that lets you write. Hockey becomes a Saturday morning thing. Hannah, who matured into being your favorite person, ends up at the same magazine for a year. You build the after on purpose.

Years later, on a long Saturday, you'll remember this day clearly — the bleachers, the lake, the friends. You'll be sitting on a porch with kids running around. You'll feel, briefly, the way you felt at twenty-one. You'll be grateful.

Hannah and you drive across the country in a beat-up car. You stop in towns you can't pronounce. You eat at diners. You take a photo at every state border. The photos live in a shoebox you never quite organize. You don't need to.
